Psychology of people who are addicted to Instagram
description:
Why can one quick check of Instagram turn into twenty minutes of scrolling you can't explain? The psychology behind compulsive Instagram use has less to do with weak willpower than most people think. It has more to do with how the brain responds to unpredictable rewards, uncomfortable feelings, and constant social comparison.

In this video, we break down why Instagram is so hard to put down and what it can quietly do to the way you see yourself. You'll see how variable rewards work, why your feed can feel like a slot machine in your pocket, and how conditioning turns a passing moment of boredom or loneliness into an automatic reach for your phone. We also look at social comparison, the way scrolling through everyone's highlight reel can make your own life feel smaller, and how likes can start to shape your mood.

Along the way, we keep the science honest. Research on social media and mood is mixed, and how someone uses the app matters a lot. This video isn't about calling Instagram evil or you broken. It's about understanding the loop so you can step out of it.

If you've ever wondered why you keep opening the app without really deciding to, this one is for you. You'll also learn a simple three-step approach, notice, name, and redirect, plus practical ways to make the app harder to reach and to build a healthier relationship with your attention.

 Join Daily Psychology: If this video helped you understand your habits a little better, like it and subscribe to Daily Psychology for more psychology breakdowns of everyday behavior.

References:

• Variable reward: the idea that unpredictable rewards can keep a behavior going more strongly than predictable ones, explained in the video through the slot machine comparison.

• Conditioning: the cue, action, and relief loop that can make a habit feel automatic.

• Social comparison: the human tendency to measure ourselves against others, and how highlight reels can intensify it.

title: Your Brain Says Yes to "Because" (Psychology Explained)
description:
Psychology explained: your brain says yes to "because", and the famous photocopier study shows how much one reason changes a no into a yes.

Lunch queue. You ask, 'Can I go first?' 'No.' At a university photocopier, 60% of people let someone skip when they just asked. When they added "because I have to make copies", a reason that says nothing at all, it jumped to 93%. A real reason ("because I'm in a rush") got 94%. But for a bigger ask, 20 pages instead of 5, the pointless reason stopped working, and only a real reason helped (Langer, Blank and Chanowitz, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1978). So give your real reason.

In my opinion, 'because' is criminally underrated. Lewisham canteen. Alfie tried, 'Oi, move.' Back of the queue. Achia asked, 'Can I go first? Because I got football at half 12.' Waved through. Your brain isn't broken. It's just old.

What's the best reason you've ever given that actually got you a yes? 👇

title: Why Everyone Else's Life Looks Better (The Highlight Reel)
description:
Everyone else's life looks better on your phone. That feeling has a name: social comparison.

In 1954, Leon Festinger proposed that we judge ourselves against other people — and we compare upward, to the ones who seem to have more. Social media is an upward-comparison machine: everyone shows their best moment. The vacation. The promotion. You never see the other ninety-nine percent. Researchers call it the highlight reel.

In 2012, Facebook users believed others are happier and have better lives — and the longer they scrolled, the stronger the belief (Chou & Edge, 2012). You are comparing your behind-the-scenes to everyone else's highlight reel. A rigged game.

In 2015, one group scrolled passively and another posted and chatted. The passive group felt worse over time. The difference was envy (Verduyn et al., 2015).

But here is the hopeful part: in 2018, students who cut social media to thirty minutes a day felt less lonely and less depressed (Hunt et al., 2018). The fix is not willpower. It is design.

title: Kenapa Kita Iri dengan Hidup Orang Lain di Media Sosial? | Otak Kita
description:
Malam hari, kamu rebahan sambil scroll ponsel, lalu berhenti di foto liburan temanmu di pantai. Pantainya biru, senyumnya lebar, ratusan orang memberi tanda suka — dan tiba-tiba hidupmu sendiri terasa biasa saja. Kenapa melihat kebahagiaan orang lain bisa membuat kita merasa kalah?

Di video ini kita bahas alasannya: teori perbandingan sosial Leon Festinger (1954) — otak kita memakai orang lain sebagai penggaris saat tidak ada ukuran yang jelas, dan iri paling tajam muncul saat orang yang dibandingkan mirip dengan kita, bidangnya penting bagi identitas kita, dan keunggulannya terasa tidak terjangkau. Lalu kenapa media sosial memperkuat iri (Chou & Edge 2012: survei 425 mahasiswa — makin lama memakai Facebook, makin merasa orang lain lebih bahagia dan hidup tidak adil; Krasnova dkk. 2013: 584 pengguna — foto liburan memicu lebih dari separuh insiden iri, pengguna pasif paling terdampak), kenapa iri itu diam-diam menggerogoti (Kross dkk. 2013: 82 orang dewasa muda, lima kali sehari selama dua minggu — makin banyak memakai Facebook, makin turun kepuasan hidup; Tandoc dkk. 2015: 736 mahasiswa — mengintip kehidupan teman memicu iri, dan iri menjadi jembatan menuju gejala depresi), dan lima langkah memakai perbandingan dengan sehat — termasuk membatasi media sosial sampai sekitar 30 menit sehari (Hunt dkk. 2018: 143 mahasiswa, tiga minggu — kesepian dan depresi berkurang secara signifikan). Di tengah video ada momen interaktif "Coba 10 detik": bayangkan postingan terakhir yang membuatmu merasa kalah.

Video baru setiap hari: hari kerja jam 18.00 WIB, akhir pekan jam 10.00 WIB. Jangan lupa subscribe channel Otak Kita supaya kamu tidak ketinggalan video berikutnya.

Sumber penelitian yang dipakai di video ini:
- Festinger, L. (1954). A theory of social comparison processes. Human Relations, 7(2), 117–140. https://doi.org/10.1177/001872675400700202
- Smith, R. H., & Kim, S. H. (2007). Comprehending envy. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 46–64. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.46
- Chou, H.-T. G., & Edge, N. (2012). "They are happier and having better lives than I am." Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking, 15(2), 117–121. https://doi.org/10.1089/cyber.2011.0324
- Krasnova, H., Wenninger, H., Widjaja, T., & Buxmann, P. (2013). Envy on Facebook: A hidden threat to users' life satisfaction? Proceedings of the 11th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik, Leipzig, Jerman.

Tuesday. 11:47 PM. Forty-seven minutes of scrolling. One engagement post. Zero of your own wins celebrated tonight.

Envy isn't the sin. That's what you've been told, and it's wrong. Envy is the signal. In this video: why comparison stings the way it does (the psychology of relative deprivation, named in 1966 — described by Marcus Aurelius 1,800 years earlier), the rigged trial your mind runs every time you scroll, the two kinds of envy (only one is poison), and the three-movement conversion that turns the sting into a compass: malicious to benign, benign to emulation, emulation to release.

You'll get the whole-life audit (Marcus's rule: compare all the parts together, not one part to one part), the conversion question (three questions that turn any envy spike into a direction), the nobody-fear cure from Epictetus (why "you will be nobody anywhere" is the real engine under your envy), and the permission slip nobody gives you: want the thing, hold the ranking loosely.

And near the end — the warning: how "staying in my lane" becomes a cage, and the 90-second return protocol for when you slip.

Then tell me which envy turned tonight — 1 for scroll envy, 2 for career envy, 3 for love-life envy. I read every word. Reply to your own comment tomorrow with your day count. Seven days of turning, and the compass points on its own. Don't enter 2027 still measuring your life against someone else's highlight reel.

🧠 THE ILLUSION OF TRANSPARENCY: Why You Think Everyone Can Read Your Mind

Have you ever felt nervous during a conversation and assumed everyone could notice it? Have you ever made a small mistake and spent hours thinking that other people were judging you?

This is the Illusion of Transparency, a fascinating cognitive bias that explains why we overestimate how easily others can recognize our internal thoughts, emotions, and feelings.

Your nervousness feels obvious to you because you're experiencing it internally. But other people cannot directly access your mind. They only see your expressions, behaviour, gestures, and words.

And here's the interesting part: what feels extremely noticeable to you might be barely noticeable to someone else.

🔍 What will you discover in this video?

• What is the Illusion of Transparency?
• Why do we think others can read our emotions?
• The famous embarrassing T-shirt experiment.
• The relationship between the Spotlight Effect and the Illusion of Transparency.
• Why nervousness feels more visible than it actually is.
• How self-focused attention influences perception.
• How this bias affects friendships and relationships.
• Why people misunderstand each other's emotions.
• How to overcome the Illusion of Transparency.

💡 A deeper psychological insight:

You experience your thoughts from the inside, but everyone else experiences you from the outside.

You know every doubt, insecurity, hesitation, and emotion happening inside your mind. Other people only see fragments of your behaviour.

Never confuse the intensity of your internal experience with how visible it is to others.

You are not as exposed as your mind sometimes makes you believe.

title: Why You Can't Stop Comparing Yourself (It's Not Envy)
description:
Why do I compare myself to everyone? It's 1 AM and you're measuring your life against strangers.
That's not envy — it's one of the oldest programs your brain runs. In 1954, Leon Festinger showed we evaluate ourselves by comparing to others (Festinger, 1954). This episode breaks down why the comparison always points upward, how social media rigs the yardstick, and what research found: heavier social-media comparison predicts lower self-esteem, driven by upward comparison (Vogel et al., 2014) — and even ten minutes of Facebook exposure can dip your mood, hardest for habitual comparers (Fardouly et al., 2015). No diagnosing, no labels — just the mechanism, and how to repoint the compass.

title: The Psychology Of Why You Stay Broke Earning More
description:
Psychology of People Who Stay Broke Even After Earning More

You doubled your income. Your bank account looks exactly the same.
This video is about the machine that made sure of it. Not a metaphor — a mechanism with three gears, each backed by published psychology and economics research: the gear that makes every raise feel normal within months, the gear that converts your neighbor's raise into your pay cut, and the gear that locks it all in with commitments you barely remember making.
You'll meet the 22 lottery winners who felt nothing, the $75,000 ceiling science is still fighting about, and the focusing illusion — the reason the whole chase may have been aimed at the wrong target.

CHAPTERS 
00:00 You doubled your income — the machine that keeps resetting yours 
01:08 The numbers nobody says out loud at dinner parties 
02:22 The 1978 lottery-winner study: the jackpot that raised nothing 
03:46 The New Normal Machine, frame by frame 
03:54 Gear 1 — Adaptation: the floor keeps moving 
04:18 Gear 2 — Comparison: the neighbor's raise 
04:40 Gear 3 — Commitment: the bars of the cage 
05:41 Five thieves mug every raise 
06:46 The $75,000 ceiling (and the scientific fight about it) 
07:41 A raise for the people around you hurts like your own pay cut 
08:23 The rich spend your money: trickle-down consumption 
09:30 The visible-goods signal: the audience decides the costume 
10:33 The focusing illusion: the chase was aimed at the wrong target 
11:29 You were never bad with money 
13:00 What was the raise that changed nothing?

STUDIES IN THIS VIDEO
Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman (1978), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — 22 lottery winners were no happier than controls and took less pleasure in ordinary things (small sample; carried with the honest correction: Lindqvist, Östling & Cesarini (2020), Review of Economic Studies — 3,362 Swedish winners: big wins durably raise life satisfaction but barely move day-to-day happiness)

Kahneman & Deaton (2010), Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — 450,000+ US responses: life evaluation keeps rising with income, but daily emotional well-being stops improving past ~$75,000 (2010 dollars); contested — Killingsworth (2021) found no plateau, and the 2023 adversarial resolution (Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers, PNAS) says the plateau holds only for the unhappiest ~15–20%

Luttmer (2005), The Quarterly Journal of Economics — neighbors' earnings rising hurts happiness about as much as your own income falling by the same amount (US couples panel, 1987–1994; correlational)

Bertrand & Morse (2016), The Review of Economics and Statistics — trickle-down consumption: middle-income families might have saved ~3% more every year if top incomes had grown at the same pace as everyone else's since the early 1980s (authors' counterfactual estimate)

Charles, Hurst & Roussanov (2009), The Quarterly Journal of Economics — visible spending (clothing, jewelry, cars) tracks the reference group's income, not your own wallet: ~25% more / ~$1,900 a year on visible goods; non-visible spending shows no such pattern

Kahneman, Krueger, Schkade, Schwarz & Stone (2006), Science — the focusing illusion: the belief that high income comes with a good mood is "widespread but mostly illusory" (interpretive synthesis, not a single experiment)

This video is for education only. It explains psychology research. It is not personal financial advice, and it does not promise any income or savings outcome.

#MoneyPsychology #PsychologyOfMoney #WealthToons#PsychToons

title: The Psychology of Comparing Yourself: Why Watching Others Win Makes You Secretly Stronger
description:
It is 11 PM. I am lying in bed, phone above my face, scrolling past a post from someone I went to school with. A promotion. A new title, a salary band I will not repeat, a photo of him shaking hands with a man in a suit, both of them grinning like the future had just signed a contract. My chest tightens. Not a lot. Just enough. And then I do the embarrassing part. I tap his profile. I scroll back. The engagement photos. The new car. The holiday in a place I cannot pronounce. I refresh the page like it owes me an answer, like the next post will explain why his life is moving and mine is standing still. I told myself I was just staying informed.

This is the psychology of comparing yourself: not proof that something is wrong with you — proof that your brain is running its oldest measuring tool on a rigged feed, and the pain is information: what you envy is a map of what you actually want, and watching others win becomes fuel the moment you change what you compare yourself to:

— Festinger's social comparison theory — humans have no built-in speedometer for life, so we measure ourselves against others; upward comparison (to those doing better) and downward comparison (to those doing worse)
— The highlight reel — you compare your behind-the-scenes to everyone else's curated cut, five best minutes of a year; survivorship bias means you only ever see the winners, never the thousands who tried and failed
— Benign vs malicious envy — the same tight chest, two directions: benign envy says "I want that too, and I'll work for it"; malicious envy says "I want them to lose it" — the feeling is not the problem, the distance is
— Self-evaluation maintenance — comparison stings most in the domains you care about most; the sting points at your values, not your worth, and it is the most honest diagnostic you own
— The comparison audit — write down who you compare yourself to, what exactly you envy, and what it costs you in minutes and mood; name the exact thing, because vague envy has no handle and specific envy is a goal
— The protocol — compare to your past self only, one year ago, not their today; compare upward only to people one step ahead, not ten; mute, don't unfollow — curate the feed like a diet; no scrolling after 10 PM
— The vow — seven days, one audit a night, one comparison to your past self every morning, one mute a day; the win is proof that it can be done, and a compass tells you which way to walk

Video #42 was about FOMO — missing out sets you free (FOMO is about missing EXPERIENCES, the fear the party is happening without you). Video #48 was about self-esteem — doubting yourself makes you invisible (the inner verdict). This one is different: it is the MEASUREMENT habit — the upward comparison loop, the highlight reel, and why watching others win can make you stronger instead of smaller. Everyone says stop comparing yourself to others and you will be happy — so why do the people who never compare themselves to anyone end up the most stuck?

📚 Research & References:
— Festinger's social comparison theory
— Upward vs downward comparison
— The highlight reel & survivorship bias
— Benign vs malicious envy
— Self-evaluation maintenance

description:
Aapka Dimaag Aapko DARA Raha Hai! 😱 | Availability Bias Explained | Thinking Fast & Slow Ch 13

क्या आपने कभी सोचा है कि एक डरावनी News देखने के बाद आपको पूरी दुनिया खतरनाक क्यों लगने लगती है? 😨

इसका कारण है हमारा दिमाग और उसकी एक खतरनाक psychological shortcut — Availability Heuristic!

इस वीडियो में हम Daniel Kahneman की bestselling book Thinking, Fast and Slow – Chapter 13: Availability, Emotion, and Risk को आसान भाषा में समझेंगे।

इस chapter में आप जानेंगे:

🧠 Availability Heuristic: हमारा दिमाग याद रहने वाली घटनाओं को ज्यादा common क्यों समझता है?

📺 Media & Fear: News और Social Media हमारी Risk Perception को कैसे प्रभावित करते हैं?

❤️ Emotion & Risk: डर, गुस्सा और भावनाएं हमारे decisions को कैसे बदलती हैं?

⚠️ Availability Cascade: कैसे एक छोटी-सी घटना पूरे समाज में डर और चिंता फैला सकती है?

💭 Affect Heuristic: हम किसी चीज को पसंद या नापसंद करने के आधार पर उसके फायदे और नुकसान का गलत आकलन क्यों करते हैं?

🔍 False Confidence: बार-बार सुनी गई बात हमें सच क्यों लगने लगती है?

इस वीडियो के अंत तक आप समझ पाएंगे कि हमारा दिमाग कई बार वास्तविक खतरे से ज्यादा उस खतरे से डरता है जिसे हम आसानी से याद कर सकते हैं।

The biggest lesson: Just because something is easy to remember doesn't mean it is likely to happen.

title: Attribution Theory: Why YOU Blame People Instead of Situations
description:
Why do you judge strangers harshly but excuse yourself? Attribution theory explains how your brain decides *why* people behave the way they do, and why it so often gets it wrong. Learn the fundamental attribution error, the actor-observer bias, and the self-serving bias, with the real experiments behind each.

In this psychology video, you'll learn:
• How Heider's shapes experiment shows we give everything a personality
• Why people still blamed a writer who was assigned his opinion (Jones & Harris, 1967)
• How a rigged quiz game made people think questioners were smarter (Ross, 1977)
• Why culture changes how strongly we blame the person over the situation
• Why seminary students walked past a man in need (Darley & Batson, 1973)
• 3 simple ways to stop judging people too quickly

title: 25 Persuasion Psychology Facts (Ethical Influence) | Psychology Explained
description:
Someone is persuading you right now — and you probably won't even notice it. From the free sample that creates a quiet debt, to the first number that secretly sets your price, to the small favor that makes people like you more — this video walks you through 25 persuasion psychology facts that explain how influence actually works.

In this video, you'll discover 25 persuasion facts, explained in plain, simple language — reciprocity, social proof, authority, scarcity, commitment and consistency, liking, framing, anchoring, the foot-in-the-door effect, the door-in-the-face effect, loss aversion, the mere exposure effect, the halo effect, priming, reactance, the decoy effect, the contrast principle, unity, the power of "because", the Benjamin Franklin effect, the cocktail party effect, the chameleon effect, the deadline effect, and the illusory truth effect. Each fact is original, grounded in well-established psychology, and paired with a real-life example you will recognize instantly. And the final fact is your best defense against all of them: knowing the trick takes away its power.

Influence is a tool — this video is about understanding it, not abusing it. Use these ideas ethically: to communicate better, to make fairer choices, and to spot it when someone else is steering you.

Have you ever been persuaded without realizing it? Comment YES or NO below. And which fact surprised you MOST?

What's inside:
1. Reciprocity — give first, and people feel they owe you
2. Social Proof — when unsure, we copy what others do
3. Authority — a title or uniform makes words feel truer
4. Scarcity — rare things feel more valuable
5. Commitment & Consistency — say yes once, and yes again feels easier
6. Liking — we say yes to people we like
7. Framing — same fact, different frame, different choice
8. Anchoring — the first number you hear sets the scale
9. Foot-in-the-Door — ask small first, the big ask follows easily
10. Door-in-the-Face — ask huge first, then ask for less
11. Loss Aversion — losing hurts more than gaining pleases
12. Mere Exposure — the more you see it, the more you like it
13. Halo Effect — one good trait makes everything else look good
14. Priming — what you just saw shapes what you do next
15. Reactance — tell people they can't, and they want it more
16. Decoy Effect — a third option steers your choice
17. Contrast — a thing looks better next to something worse
18. Unity — "people like us" persuade better than strangers
19. The Power of "Because" — a reason, even a weak one, opens doors
20. Benjamin Franklin Effect — ask a favor, and they like you more
21. Your Name Grabs You — your name cuts through any crowd
22. Chameleon Effect — mirroring builds instant rapport
23. Deadlines — a deadline turns "maybe later" into "now"
24. Repetition Feels True — hear it often enough, and it feels true
25. The Defense — knowing these tricks is your best defense

title: The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel: The Core Ideas Explained
description:
Doing well with money has a lot less to do with what you know and a lot more to do with how you behave. That's the entire argument of Morgan Housel's The Psychology of Money, and it might be the most useful finance book you read this decade.

In this video, we break down the core ideas from the book: why nobody's actually being irrational once you understand their money story, why ambition without a stopping point wrecks people, why getting rich and staying rich require completely different skills, why what people show you about their wealth is almost never what they actually have, why the real payoff of money is control over your time, why you should plan on being wrong, and why your savings rate matters more than almost anything else you can control.

Every example in this video uses invented people and numbers to illustrate the concepts, not the book's actual case studies, so you can see the math without us just repeating Housel's stories back to you.

This is a curated look at the book's core ideas, not a full chapter-by-chapter breakdown. If you want to go deeper, the book itself is short and well worth the read.

title: How to stop comparing yourself to others : 3 questions that help
description:
How to stop comparing yourself with others? Why do we compare ourselves to other people even when we know it makes us feel worse? And how do we stop comparison from convincing us that someone else’s success means we’re falling behind?


Maybe you’ve scrolled past someone’s promotion, vacation, beautiful home, successful children, or seemingly put-together life and suddenly started questioning your own. Nothing about your life changed—but somehow, it feels like less.






In this episode of the Ambitious on My Terms Podcast, Kim Patten explores why we compare ourselves, the psychology behind social comparison, and why comparison itself isn’t always the problem. Sometimes it can actually reveal what we want, value, or hope to change. The trouble starts when “she’s doing well” becomes “she’s better than me.” 






You’ll learn how to recognize when your brain is filling in the blanks about someone else’s life, how to separate facts from the story you’re creating, and how to use comparison as information instead of evidence that you aren’t enough. Kim also shares a simple three-question practice you can use the next time you find yourself caught in a comparison spiral. 


Because the goal isn’t to never compare yourself again. It’s to stop letting comparison determine your worth.






In this episode, you’ll explore:

  •  ​Why humans naturally compare themselves to others
  •  ​How social media can intensify upward comparison
  •  ​When comparison can actually be healthy or useful
  •  ​How envy can reveal something you genuinely want or value
  •  ​Why high-achieving women can get trapped using someone else’s “scorecard”
  •  ​A simple practice for interrupting comparison before it becomes self-judgment
  •  ​How to admire another woman without diminishing yourself





If you’ve ever wondered, “Why does everyone else seem to have it together except me?” this episode is for you.


You don’t have to be better than her to be enough. You already are.

title: Newton’s Bitter War With His Greatest Rival
description:
Your coworker just got promoted. You smile, shake their hand and say “you deserve it.” And somewhere in the back of your mind, a small voice asks: why not me?

In this episode of The Mechanism, we go back to London in the late 1600s and the bitter rivalry between Isaac Newton and Robert Hooke: a dispute over light, gravity and credit that never healed. Centuries later, there’s still no confirmed portrait of Hooke, and a legend grew up around why. We look at what’s documented, what isn’t, and why so many people were ready to believe it.

Then we turn to the psychology underneath: social comparison, why the brain treats status like a resource, why social media makes it worse, and what stories from The Lion King to Vikings understand about the difference between feeling envy and acting on it.

title: Why You Always Compare Yourself to Others (It's Not Jealousy)
description:
You scroll for two minutes and suddenly your whole life feels behind. It isn't really jealousy. Your brain is trying to measure itself, and it's using a broken ruler.
This is the story of Daniel, his college friend Chris, and a phone call at two in the morning that changed what Daniel thought he was looking at. We look at social comparison theory, why everyone else seems happier than they are, and how to pick a better ruler.

description:
You scroll for five minutes and suddenly your life feels small. Comparing ourselves to others is wired deep into how humans think. Here's why we do it, why social media makes it worse, what the research says about cutting back, and how to turn comparison into something useful.

0:00 Intro
0:15 Social Comparison
0:46 Up And Down

2:41 How To Compare Better

Sources:
- Festinger, Human Relations 1954 (a theory of social comparison processes)
- Verduyn et al., Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 2015 (passive Facebook use undermines well-being through envy)
